issues.issue: The letter styles the document as a "response to your request for proposal for underwriting services" while promising "broad based, high quality investment banking services," leaving open whether it is a binding undertaking or a solicitation; that question cannot be answered without the Broker-Dealer Agreement's Section 5.4 entire-agreement clause, which says the deal documents contain the entire agreement and that there are "no other representations, endorsements, promises, agreements or understandings, oral, written or inferred." Read with Section 5.10 (no implied duties on any party beyond those expressly set out), the proposal's promissory language and the later agreement cannot both be given full effect.

"Unparalleled auction rate performance" (with "excel at" and "well suited") is an unmeasurable superlative with no benchmark, and it is unclear whether it describes Goldman's past record or promises how Presbyterian's own auctions would perform. A court would have to decide whether the phrase is actionable promise or non-actionable puffery.

"We hope that this proposal helps to demonstrate the commitment and depth of services that we are prepared to provide" is hedged aspiration ("hope," "prepared to," "would make for") with no identified services, standard or duration for the "long-term relationship." Whether "commitment" imports an enforceable obligation to continue providing services is the ambiguity.

The provision enumerates specific "key services" — remarketing and auction agent services, counterparty on derivatives, liquidity and credit support, underwriting — but the answering text describes only the firm's general size, history and staffing, so it is unclear which of the listed services Goldman was representing it would supply as opposed to merely being capable of. The tension between the itemized list and the generic response is what a court would construe.

"Complete, broad based, intensive coverage ... regardless of where they are in their capital cycle" and "focusing on what is best for the client rather than what produces the next trade" set no ascertainable content or standard of performance. Whether these words create any measurable service obligation, or are sales rhetoric, is the ambiguity.

"Our clients' interests always come first" is urged as imposing a client-first (quasi-fiduciary) duty, which cannot be squared with the Broker-Dealer Agreement's Section 5.10 ("Nothing contained in this Broker-Dealer Agreement, the Indenture or the Auction Agreement shall be deemed to imply any duties, covenants or obligations ... not otherwise expressly set forth") or with Section 2.1(d), which permits the broker-dealer to participate in Auctions for its own account. The two instruments give conflicting answers on whether Goldman owed Presbyterian a duty to subordinate its own trading interests.

The statement that services rendered "on an ongoing basis" to other systems are "similar to those sought by Presbyterian" uses an undefined comparator ("similar") and an open-ended list ending in "strategic advisory services." Whether it represents that the same ongoing services would be furnished to Presbyterian is unclear.

"Leader and innovator in each of the service areas desired by Presbyterian" is an unmeasurable claim, and the enumerated areas — including "auction agent/broker-dealer services" and "use of credit enhancement" — read against the following sentence about an "integrated ... capital management strategy" leave it uncertain whether Goldman is describing competence or undertaking to deliver each listed area. That gap between the specific list and the general integration promise is what would be construed.

The provision opens with a truncated, garbled heading ("FORMATION STRATEGI") and mis-rendered text ("optimal cost of capitat"), so the subject to which "we take the long view of capital formation" attaches is not identifiable from the words. The mechanical defect leaves the scope of the described "integrated approach" indeterminate.

"The central tool used in providing this service" has no clear antecedent for "this service" within the provision, so what service the CSM Model is promised for is uncertain. The added statement that the model is used "for the firm's largest and most prestigious" clients gives no criterion for whether Presbyterian would receive it.

The provision is framed entirely in capability terms — the model "can assist," "has the capability" — so it is unclear whether Goldman undertook actually to run these analyses for Presbyterian or merely described what the tool could do. "Optimal" debt and investment portfolios is likewise given no defined measure.
